title: Share Incentive Plans: Types, Tax Advantages and When to Participate
summary: A share incentive plan is an employer program that gives employees company stock for free, at a discount or as part of their compensation. Here's what to know.
body_markdown:
A share incentive plan is an employer program that gives employees company stock for free, at a discount or as part of their compensation. In the U.S., common arrangements include employee stock purchase plans, restricted stock units, stock options and employee stock ownership plans. Each has its own eligibility rules, vesting requirements and tax treatment. This article explains how these plans work, their potential tax advantages and what to consider before participating; limits should be verified before publication.


A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=sma__falc_relevant&utm_content=whatisashareincentiveplan) can review any compensation plans, including stock options, to help you determine the best fit for your long-term goals.


## How Share Incentive Plans Work


Employers use share incentive plans to reward employees and link part of their compensation to the company’s performance. Employees may receive shares through grants, buy them with payroll deductions, or earn them through employer contributions. Awards often[vest over time](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/vesting-period) , meaning employees earn the right to keep the shares or use their options after meeting conditions, such as staying with the company for several years.


A grant is the award itself. For example, an employer might grant you 100 stock options. Vesting determines when you earn the right to use them; if one-quarter vests each year, you could exercise 25 options after the first year. Exercising means using an option to buy shares at its set price.


In an employee stock purchase plan, the offering period is the time when payroll deductions accumulate before the plan buys shares, such as a six-month period. A[holding period](https://smartasset.com/investing/what-is-the-average-stock-holding-period) is the time you must keep shares to meet a plan rule or qualify for certain tax treatment. Plan documents explain eligibility, contribution limits, vesting, sale restrictions and what happens if you leave. Some plans are available only to specific employee groups, so review the terms before enrolling.


## Types of Share Incentive Plans


An[employee stock purchase plan (ESPP)](https://smartasset.com/taxes/is-employee-stock-purchase-plan-pre-tax) lets eligible employees use payroll deductions to buy company shares, often at a discount. In a qualified Section 423 plan, the option price may be as low as 85% of the stock’s fair market value, effectively a 15% discount. The law also limits the value of stock an employee can purchase under these plans to $25,000 per calendar year, measured using fair market value when the option is granted. Actual plan terms may offer a smaller discount or lower limits.


Restricted stock units (RSUs) are promises to deliver shares or their cash value after vesting.[Incentive stock options (ISOs) and nonqualified stock options (NSOs)](https://smartasset.com/taxes/isos-vs-nsos-how-are-they-taxed-differently) give employees the right to buy shares at a specified price; ISOs must meet specific tax rules, while NSOs generally do not receive the same treatment. An[employee stock ownership plan (ESOP)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/esop-vs-401k) is a qualified retirement plan that invests primarily in the employer’s stock and allocates shares to participant accounts.


Plan Type How You Get Shares Vesting or Holding Rules When Tax Generally Applies


ESPP Buy through payroll deductions, often at a discount Offering and tax holding periods may apply Usually when shares are sold; tax treatment depends on whether the sale qualifies


[RSUs](https://smartasset.com/investing/what-is-a-restricted-stock-unit-rsu) Shares are delivered after vesting Vesting schedule set by employer Ordinary income when shares vest


ISOs Exercise an option to buy shares Must meet employment and holding requirements for potential tax benefits Generally when shares are sold; exercise may trigger AMT


NSOs Exercise an option to buy shares Vesting schedule; holding period begins after exercise in common cases Ordinary income on the spread at exercise; later gain or loss when shares are sold


ESOPs Employer contributions allocate shares to a retirement account Plan vesting and distribution rules apply Generally deferred until distribution, subject to tax rules


## Tax Advantages of Share Incentive Plans


Some ESPP shares and ISOs may qualify for[long-term capital gains](https://smartasset.com/taxes/2021-capital-gains-tax-rates) treatment if the employee meets required holding periods. For ESPPs, a qualifying sale generally occurs after the later of one year from the share purchase or two years from the option grant. A disqualifying sale can make some of the discount ordinary income.


RSUs are generally taxed as ordinary income when they vest, while NSOs generally create ordinary income when exercised based on the difference between the share value and exercise price. Exercising ISOs may trigger the[alternative minimum tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/amt-tax-brackets) . ESOP participants generally defer taxes until they receive a distribution, subject to plan and tax rules.


Consider a hypothetical ESPP in which an employee contributes $10,000 to buy shares at 85% of their market value. The purchase-day market value is about $11,765, so the discount is about $1,765. Assume the grant-date and purchase-date values make that $1,765 the relevant discount for tax purposes.


Hypothetical Step Calculation Amount


Employee’s purchase cost Given $10,000


[Market value](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/market-value) at purchase $10,000 ÷ 0.85 About $11,765


Discount at purchase $11,765 − $10,000 About $1,765


Qualifying sale at $13,000 $13,000 proceeds − $10,000 cost $3,000 total gain


Qualifying sale: ordinary income portion Lesser of $1,765 discount or $3,000 gain About $1,765


Qualifying sale: remaining capital gain $3,000 − $1,765 About $1,235


Disqualifying sale at $11,765 $11,765 proceeds − $10,000 cost About $1,765 ordinary income; no additional gain


This simplified example assumes the plan meets Section 423 rules and ignores fees and other tax details. The actual ordinary-income amount depends on grant, purchase and sale dates, and share values.


## When to Participate in a Share Incentive Plan


Weigh the plan’s discount or employer contribution against your[cash flow](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/cash-flow-planning) , existing exposure to your employer and how long you expect to stay. With an employee stock purchase plan offering a 15% discount, for example, compare the potential savings with the amount deducted from each paycheck and any limits on when you can sell. Don’t contribute money you may need for near-term expenses.


Selling shares soon after an ESPP purchase can help capture the discount while limiting how long you’re exposed to changes in the stock price. But the sale may not qualify for favorable tax treatment. Holding long enough to meet the required tax holding periods may improve the[tax liability](https://smartasset.com/taxes/tax-liability) in some cases, but it also leaves you exposed to a possible decline in the share price.


Your plans for your job matter, too. If you may leave within a year, check how departure affects unvested awards, payroll deductions and the deadline to exercise vested options. If your paycheck, retirement plan or[brokerage account](https://smartasset.com/investing/best-brokerage-accounts) already depends heavily on your employer, adding more company stock could increase that concentration. Review the plan documents and consider whether the potential benefits fit your financial goals and risk tolerance.


## Bottom Line


Share incentive plans can boost compensation through discounted shares, stock grants or employer contributions, and some may offer tax advantages. But vesting rules, taxes, cash needs and the risk of tying both your job and investments to one company matter. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/us-top-financial-advisors) can help you decide how much to participate, when to sell and how employer stock fits your broader plan.
